abstract.t: This document defines two CBOR "simple" values to be used as unique (reserved) labels in a CBOR map holding an embedded signature construct.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This document defines two CBOR "simple" values to be used as unique (reserved) labels in conjunction with an embedded signature scheme described in Appendix E of CBOR::Core , from now on referred to as CSF (CBOR Signature Format).
The purpose of the unique labels is to securely decouple application-specific labels from the CSF signature container, respectively hold data that should be excluded from the signature.
In addition to eliminating the need for application-specific labels for embedded signature constructs, the net result includes simplified signature APIs as well.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Enhanced (Current) Solution
section.t: In the following sample (copied from ), a CBOR simple(99) value is used as a reserved label for the embedded signature container:
The advantages with using simple(99) include:

ul.li: Eliminates the need for application-specific labels for signature containers.

Using deterministic encoding (a CSF prerequisite), CBOR simple types lexicographically follow after other CBOR elements (of the kind normally used as labels). This makes sense for embedded signatures, since they usually "attest" the application data that is (list-wise), situated above the signature container, like in the example.

section.name: Unsigned Data Option
section.t: In use-cases like when issuing selectable disclosures (e.g. as in ), it may be advantageous being able to carry unsigned data together with signed data, as an alternative to a more elaborate construct. For this purpose, the reserved CBOR simple(100) label was introduced:

section.name: Constrained System CSF Verifier
section.t: The following C sample code shows how the use of simple(99), due to the deterministic coding rules, makes the actual signature value appear as the last item in a CSF-signed object.
This arrangement enables embedded signatures based on the CSF scheme, to be applied to quite primitive systems, with moderate additional resource requirements.
Note: this is a low-level solution, relying on the assumption that floating-point numbers are not used as labels, since such labels would appear after the simple(99) label.
